In the past I think Newfoundland has suffered from the fact that too little capital has been available for investment in the fisheries. Today we realize that more fish plants are necessary. There is a need for modern fresh fish plants which will take the fish from the fishermen as they come in, split them, freeze them and get them ready for the most productive market, or in other words the market which would produce the largest number of dollars for our fishermen. To us, of course, that is the great United States market.
There was a time when Newfoundland was producing over a million quintals of codfish, most of which was salted. Today, however, we realize that many of our customers who used to buy our fish are producing their own. That has been especially so since the war. Of course, during the war there was little difficulty in disposing of fish. The. greatest problem in those days was transportation. It was easy then to sell fish, provided the transportation was available. We now see that these people who used to buy our fish in days gone by are, as I said before, producing their own. They come to the Grand Banks and look for fish. The result is that we are not able to sell such a large quantity of fish as used to be sold in days gone by.
As far as the Labrador fishery is concerned, I think something special will have to be done. This is not the first time that I have brought to the attention of the minister of fisheries-not the present minister but his immediate predecessor-the need for something being done for the Labrador fisheries. There is a long section of the Labrador coast line where there is an abundant fishery. In fact, as to the fishery around the island of Belle Isle-a large producing area-I understand that at one time in Paris, France, berths for Belle Isle were drawn. That fact shows that in those days when the French were fishing on the French shore-the treaty coast, as we call it even today-there was an abundance of fish around this section. It is still a large-producing section. We realize that those who go there in schooners have gone to great expense in providing themselves with vessels and gear, and that they get an abundant harvest of fish. But the market for the Labrador fish is not what it used to be. Costs of twine, netting and other equipment have gone up to such an extent that there is not much money in fishing. The result is that many people have given up fishing on the Labrador.

Supply-Fisheries
As Labrador is in my riding I should like to mention another matter of which I learned during this past summer when I was visiting the Labrador coast. I refer to the great scarcity of salt which existed during last year. I think something special will have to be done in the way of providing salt depots for the Labrador. I believe this is a matter which will have to be looked into. As we know there was the royal commission on fishery development which was investigating fisheries and which brought in its report last year. This report is being implemented. I hope that something will be done to see that salt depots are provided so that when the fish are at hand the fishermen will have a ready source of salt which will enable them to preserve the fish. In that way they will be able to have some earning power. Fishing, of course, is practically the only means of employment they can have in the summertime.
At La Scie, at which I believe a large plant is to be installed, there is also available a large catch for the fishermen. In the past they have had to salt their catch, thus getting, so to speak, a much smaller earning power than would be available to them if a filleting plant were in operation there. With the implementation of the recommendation of the report of the Walsh fishery development commission I believe that there will now be installed in Newfoundland some of these up-to-date plants which will look after, not only the filleting of the fresh fish, or the utilization of the fish in the fresh state, but will also, by modern up-to-date dryers, take care of some of the salt fish which requires to be cured.
There was a time in Newfoundland when most of the fish drying was done on the flakes, a great deal of it being done by the women of Newfoundland. In those days there was quite an art in making good fish. I noticed that this afternoon the minister emphasized the quality of fish. In those days, provided the weather was good and the climate favourable, there was no lack of good merchantable fish. But, unfortunately, it seems that in the last few years the export of merchantable fish, the best quality fish, has fallen off to a considerable degree.
The fishery, which means so much to our fishermen and which, as I said before, is the only means of livelihood for many of these people, is being looked after, and I think the provision of loans for fishermen is most necessary. These men do not have a great amount of money. They need dollars in order to procure gear and fishing boats, and an opportunity should be afforded them to obtain loans more easily in order that they may equip themselves to catch fish.

Emphasis was placed this afternoon on the question of conservation, and it is most essential. The international treaties are of mutual advantage. The Grand Banks are and have been throughout the centuries a most important reservoir of food and we should realize that there is great need for conservation of the supply so that throughout the centuries to come the fish will be available that are so essential and necessary to provide the protein that our people need.
Then there is the question of the great seal herds that come south each year and are found off the strait of Belle Isle. During the past few months several vessels have been prosecuting the seal fishery. Unfortunately there have been some losses and the catch this year was not very good. We are very thankful that the government has provided an aerial survey so that statistics can be gathered respecting the quantity of seals available. I should like to point out the great loss to our nation in the past through allowing carcasses of seal meat to go to the bottom of the ocean when they could have provided good edible food for our population. In fact the kidneys and livers of young seals are very nutritive. I think that there should be further study of the sealing industry in order that there may be utilization not only of the pelts, the seal oil, fat and skins which in the past the fishermen have been in the habit of bringing to port, but also of the by-products so that the greatest possible benefit may be derived from these materials which are our natural heritage and which in the past have gone to waste.
Today the oil markets are depressed. The demand for oil seems to be very small. We realize also that the introduction of plastics has affected the production of leather goods. Air travel has created a need for very light luggage. This of course has reacted against the leather trade and has brought into being new synthetic materials. This has affected the livelihood of those people who engaged in catching seals for their pelts and skins and to whom the industry meant so much.
I should also like to refer to the whaling industry which is also practically extinct in Newfoundland. However, I think that perhaps a closed season is all to the good. When whale oil is so low in value it is better to let the whales go and allow them to increase until the market for oil becomes better. The territorial limits for our fishermen need to be extended and the interests of our shore fishermen protected to the utmost extent.
The delegation which will be going to Europe will be trying to bring about additional sales in our codfish markets of Portugal, Spain and Italy. We are glad to know

that the Minister of Public Works is going along and we believe that he will do a good job. There was a time when we used a lot of Spanish salt to salt our fish. When I was a boy it was a common sight to see barques, brigantines and other vessels, some of which had been built in Wales at Portmadoc, coming into port with cargoes of salt from Cadiz in Spain and from Cagliari in Italy, but today we get a lot of our salt from the West Indies rather than from European countries.
Then there is the matter of nets and Italian hemp. As we know, nylon is quite expensive. It makes a good net and good cordage, but in the old days we used a lot of Italian hemp. Perhaps that is a matter that the delegation will look into to see whether or not we might not be able to get more of that hemp from Italy because, as we are all aware, rope is a very important article in the catching of codfish. It seems to me that we must be prepared to utilize the great resources that lie at our doorstep. Today we see Russian trawlers coming to our banks to fish and Norwegian steamers steaming to our icefields. We see the value of the harvest which nature has so bountifully provided for our use slipping away from us to be used to provide products which will enter into competition with our own exports, thus further restricting the markets which we can supply.
At this point I should like to say a word to the fishermen of Newfoundland who endure such hardships in the fisheries. I would point out that so far as the Newfoundland fishermen are concerned-I do not suggest this is limited to Newfoundland-their interests are being well looked after by the Minister of Fisheries. In addition we have as our cabinet representative the Secretary of State. I am assured that everything possible will be done, in co-operation with the minister who is responsible for Newfoundland's cabinet work, to assist our fishermen in every possible way.
The prosperity of the fishing industry is dependent upon exports and world trade. Our home market is relatively small, and the loss of the world markets would deal a severe blow to the industry. Thus we see that we are in need of a more aggressive trade policy. The marketing problem is not an easy one. We are extremely thankful for the great work that has been done by the fisheries department in the marketing of the catch of Newfoundland fish, in co-operation with NAFEL. We realize the serious problem presented in the sterling area where so many of our competitors have sterling balances by means of which they can exchange their products and get other products as well. Today in Newfoundland we are dependent
Supply-Fisheries
upon the Canadian dollar. When our customers are short of dollars, we find it is not so easy to market our fish.
The expansion that is envisaged in the Newfoundland fishery is not a mirage. It is there, so to speak, right on the horizon. The transition from salt fish to fresh fish is being realized today, and we are aware of the additional revenue that will place in the hands of our fishermen. As we get more plants, we realize there will be more employment and our fishery will have an increasing export value. We shall have an increased ability to compete in the world markets. The export markets we are able to supply are limited because of exchange difficulties, when compared with other countries that have no currency problem.
As I said before, the frozen fish markets are more lucrative markets and with the improvement in technique and lower costs we shall be in a better position to compete with other people. We are only too anxious to supply those markets that we regard as necessary if our fishermen are to maintain the standard of living we feel is necessary for them. Unfortunately, in Newfoundland there is too little hydro power. If there were a greater hydro development I feel we would be able to instal more mechanical fish driers and thus lower our costs. It would also relieve the fishermen from so much of this backbreaking work of spreading the fish on their flakes. I feel that we can be most optimistic in our outlook for the fisheries.
Personally, I have great faith in our fisheries. While in the past there have been problems which seemingly would engulf us, today we are in a better position. We can look upon the future with more hope and a better realization of our great heritage. We must put forth a united effort in striving towards this goal, with a firm faith in our ability to achieve success and full prosperity in the great fishing industry.

While listening to this discussion, Mr. Chairman, it struck me that within the past few years our fisheries have become rather important to the government, and have received considerable attention. I can recall the time in this house when there were perhaps two of us, and I was one, who took part in this debate. The reason was that up until the appointment of the Hon. Mr. Mayhew I thought that the fisheries department was a place in which a member was put to get him ready for appointment to the cabinet sometime if he showed promise. The result was that not much was done about fisheries.
Listening to the minister this afternoon, with his comprehensive survey, it was rather

Supply-Fisheries
encouraging. He has taken hold of a department with which he was unfamiliar when he started. Today he exhibited a good grasp of the subject, to the extent that I feel he has disarmed practically everyone who had some criticism to make. While the minister is entitled to all the credit we can give him, we must not forget that the minister cannot do the job alone. A good minister, and a smart minister, will always have smart men around him. The smart men around him, like the deputy minister, cannot do very much either unless the minister has some intelligence and some flexibility. It appears that the fisheries department is now fortunate in having that combination. They have a team that is working. There is no doubt but that the whole industry will benefit from this.
Listening to the last speaker I was struck by the fine speech he made and I want to agree with him about expanding the Unemployment Insurance Act to take in the fishing industry. We have had this subject up in the house on a good many occasions. The Minister of Fisheries does not have jurisdiction in so far as that question is concerned, but he could use his good offices and his persuasive powers upon the Minister of Labour to make sure consideration is given to bringing these fishermen under the Unemployment Insurance Act. The last speaker made a good survey of the fisheries in Newfoundland. He said he could look forward with a great deal of optimism to the future. I do not want to be a wet blanket but it is going to take more than optimism to solve the problem for the fishing industry.
For the past number of years the fishing industry has been going through much the same change as most industries in Canada, and that is a technological change. The fishing industry is becoming a mechanized industry, and that is true all over the world. There is more and more fish being produced. Before the minister puts his estimates in final form, there is something I should like him to look at and comment upon.
A good deal of our fish production goes to the United States. This evening's news indicates that the United States is giving authority to those responsible for imports and exports to set up quotas and/or tariffs on fish. Well, it is going to take more than optimism to get around that. If a country that takes a large share of our fish is arriving at the conclusion that it can solve its problems by fencing itself in, by putting up tariffs and embargoes against imports from this country, such action of course can be followed only by retaliation and chaos so far as international marketing is concerned.

Before the conclusion of his estimates I would ask the minister to take a look at the proposals made within the last few hours by the United States to see how it will affect our industry in Canada. I am concerned about this because a large share of the fish caught on the east coast goes to the United States. While my own home town is recognized as a mining town, there is also at that point a large sword fishing industry valued at about $2 million a year. Almost the total catch goes to the United States. I am wondering if the attempt in that country to fence themselves in, so far as fish, lead, zinc and other commodities are concerned, will militate against the continuing of the industry as it is today, to say nothing about its expansion.
That was my principal reason for speaking at this time. In the final analysis the minister and his department are up against the question of world trade. While he has done an excellent job in making the people of Canada fish conscious, more can be done. I believe it is correct to say that more information has been disseminated among the people of Canada from his department during the past couple of years than has ever happened before in the history of this country. That has been good work, and there can be no doubt that while we wish to build up our own home market we depend largely upon the export market.
With trends as we see them today there is a possibility that we may run into some difficulties. Many valuable things have been done by the Department of Fisheries during the minister's term of office. The finalizing of the agreements in the Pacific and the Atlantic, and the setting up of these commissions were things that were badly needed. It was also a great honour for Canada when the deputy minister of fisheries was selected to head one of these commissions. I believe this is an indication that perhaps Canada is paying more practical attention to the problem than any other country. I believe it is generally recognized and appreciated that our deputy minister is just about the last word, so far as a knowledge of fisheries is concerned. Of course there is a very good reason for that: He got most of his practical education from the standpoint of administration in Nova Scotia. Then, like many others from that part of the country, he has had to go far afield to demonstrate his ability. A good job is being done in formulating the kind of organization that not only protects the industry and assists in marketing, but also adds to the general education on the subject. The machinery is in good hands, and it is clear that some planning is being made in connection with the whole question of production and marketing, as well as technological changes, and all that sort of thing.

However all this is not going to do much good unless we can sell the fish we catch. I would appreciate it if before we finish discussion on the fisheries estimates the minister would give an analysis of what is going on in the United States, with particular reference to its relationship to the future of our fishing industry.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the discussion that has taken place, and the comments made by so many hon. members, I shall endeavour to make my comments brief. However there are two or three observations I should like to make.
May I say at the outset that a year or so ago the Minister of Fisheries visited the constituency of Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare; in fact he visited on two different occasions. On each occasion he made an excellent impression, not only on the members of the fishing industry but also upon the fishermen in the boats. He talked with many of them, and they felt that there was at the head of the Department of Fisheries a man who was really interested in their problems. I do feel the excellent presentation he made this afternoon, when he gave a resume of the work of the department during the last year as well as an outline of future plans for expansion, research, inspection and the like, was such as to make hon. members realize more than ever how fortunate we are that the Minister of Fisheries is a man of the calibre of the present incumbent.
Last year when we were discussing the fisheries estimates those of us from the fishing constituencies were extremely worried about the marketing situation. However we went through that bad period. We know the situation has been getting better, and we know also that right now it is much better than it has been for some considerable time. When I was home at Easter, and on another occasion three weeks before that, I talked with many persons engaged in the fishing industry. They told me that some of the markets were improving, that others had improved a great deal, and that they looked for improvement in other directions. There was an altogether different spirit to that I had noted in the previous year. Those of us from Nova Scotia are particularly pleased that it should be our own Nova Scotian minister (Mr. Winters) who should be heading the delegation to the Mediterranean countries with a view to improving markets in that area.
I was greatly pleased by the description the minister gave of the method of manufacturing fish sticks. I know many people are asking what these fish sticks are. His explanation was clear, brief, and concise,
Supply-Fisheries
and I believe it will mean that people throughout Canada who will read about the speech he has made will have a better idea of what this product is, and that it will lead to further sales. It appears to us that the manufacture of fish sticks is going to mean a great deal in increasing the consumption of fish.
I recall that two years ago when speaking in this debate I was very much upset about the loss of fishing gear, particularly boats and lobster traps. I remember that on that occasion members in all parties spoke about the need for some form of insurance or indemnity plan. Last year, when the estimates were discussed just before the close of the session we had very little time to speak about the matter, other than to thank the minister for having introduced the plan. I would like to say that although it was received with some doubt, as is usual in connection with any new plan, I have found upon talking to fishermen in my constituency that more and more are accepting it, and are finding it most helpful. I would appreciate it if, before the discussion is completed, the minister would give us some idea of the number of fishermen who have applied for coverage, and those who have applied for an indemnity because of losses they have suffered. I believe that in a free enterprise economy the setting up of some sort of indemnity plan is by far the best procedure.
I do know that many fishermen in my area are pleased with it, and I am sure that as time goes on we will find most of them will seek this form of coverage.
I speak of the insurance plan particularly as it covers boats and lobster traps. I would ask the minister if at a later time he would give us some idea of the success of the new metal lobster traps. I know that in the first instance there were fishermen who felt that lobsters would not enter a trap unless it was made of laths. I am now given to understand that the lobster is not so particular, and that he will enter a metal trap if it is the right shape and the right size, provided it contains the necessary bait. I know experiments have been carried on, and I would appreciate his telling the committee as to their success or otherwise, and whether the cost can be brought down to a point where metal traps would compete with traps made of laths.
I mention problems concerning lobsters particularly because the constituency of Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare, which I have the honour to represent, is the constituency which does an exceptionally large lobster business. In fact, it is in that constituency in the course of a year, during those months of the lobster season from December 1 to May 31, that about 10 million pounds of lobsters

Supply-Fisheries
are caught, which are shipped to the United States. The net return to the fishermen is $4 million or more for that amount of lobsters, and it is new money that comes into the country. Not only that, but it is that constituency-I may be pardoned if I mention such a fact-in Nova Scotia which in point of production, that is in poundage and dollars, does a larger fish business than any other constituency in the province.
On other occasions when I have spoken on the fisheries estimates I have referred to this anomaly which we have on the coast of Nova Scotia because of our two limits, the three-mile limit for draggers of all other nations but our own, and the twelve-mile limit for our own draggers. This means that there is an area of water from the three-mile limit to the twelve-mile limit; in other words, there is a nine-mile preserve for fishermen of every country but our own. I have discussed this with departmental officials; X have read articles about it; I know of the troubles of defining territorial waters, but I do hope that the studies that are being carried on at the moment may lead to some solution to this problem so that our fishermen are not penalized as they are at the present time. In other words, it appears as though all of us should have a twelve-mile limit, or all should have a three-mile limit.
There is one other point that always comes up when draggers are mentioned. The inshore fishermen continually complain of the wastage of draggers. I know that in the past I have been told that the wastage is only 5 per cent or 10 per cent, but the fishermen tell me that sometimes it runs as high as 50 per cent. I do not know how one can prove the percentages. The larger meshes that are being used will of course make some improvement. I understand a great deal of that is being done voluntarily, but to the best of my knowledge there is no international decision that there shall be an increase in the size of the mesh.
I promised to be brief, Mr. Chairman. May I ask the minister when he speaks again to tell us of the success of the steel traps, and make some comments about the problem, particularly along our coast, with respect to the three-mile and the twelve-mile limit. Then, I should like him to give us some idea as to the success of the insurance or indemnity plan for traps and boats.

Mr. Chairman, it is a very bold thing for a man from an inland town to try to venture into a talk on fisheries. We have some water in Greenwood. We have a little river that runs through it called the Don, and some of you have passed over it, but I 
would not willingly give my Liberal opponent in the next election any fish that came out of the water to which I have referred.
Really the only excuse that I have for getting to my feet is to come to the protection of the minister. I come to his protection before he is completely swamped, flooded, overwhelmed by the avalanche, the cataract, of praise which he has received. But it is not because I could not join in it. I was not able to hear the minister's speech but I went and read it in Hansard. I found it very interesting. But I think there is really a limit to everything, and I thought I would at least give him a few minutes' respite. He thanks me, and I am grateful that he does.
There is another thing that occurred to me, too. It is a matter of regret that I see that the Secretary of State is not in his seat. It seems to me a great pity that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is not going to take part in this debate because we have heard sagas of his election. We have heard echoes of his addressing audiences on the shore with a heaving stomach from heaving ships, and I do feel that he should be heard. It seems to me it will be too bad if he does not speak in this debate. Why, it would be as if a man from Toronto did not refer to the subway; as if an hon. member from Saskatchewan did not speak of the Saskatchewan river and the pollution thereof; as if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did not take part in a debate on pensions.
Having said that, I just want to come back for a minute not to criticize but really on the minister's behalf to express relief that apparently there is still something left for him to do. As I listened to some of the speeches I felt that he was like the Creator with nothing left for him to do except to survey his work and say that it was good.
As time went on I began to see that there are things to do, and it greatly relieved me because I am sure the minister is industrious and he does not want to have time hanging heavy on his hands. As I listened to the speeches I felt sure at first the situation must be that the price of fish had ascended inconceivably high; that the costs had gone inconceivably low; that the profits were inconceivably great. I am not quite sure that is so. The minister will tell us when he comes to speak further.
I have gathered, as I listened to the speeches, that there are some things still to do. I gathered that the kidneys and liver of young seals still need some study. That is a matter for the minister to concern himself with. I gathered the price of twine is not all that it might be, and I did gather also that there is such a question as international trade,

and it is on that, that I should like to ask the minister just one question. I read his speech carefully enough, and I did not observe that he said anything in it about Brazil. He mentioned several other countries, but he did not mention Brazil. I noted also that the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay did point out that the trade in Newfoundland was not nearly as great as it used to be, and I gathered that Brazil used to be one of its great markets.
In that connection I just want to raise the question in general so that the minister can explain it to us. When he comes to that he might perhaps in his stride explain the statement which was made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who I gather has now taken over the trade aspect of matters, in a speech made last February, in which he said something that I could not understand and which has never been explained yet. The minister said, as reported at page 2105 of Hansard:
Today I was reminded that our sales to South America are off, and it was suggested that my trip may be the reason.
Hon. members will recall that the Minister of Trade and Commerce made a trip to Brazil early in 1953, and most of us had the idea that he went down there in order to try to increase trade with Brazil. It is a fact that when he came back there was a rather remarkable falling off. The minister explained that in a way which was really something. I pass this on now to the Minister of Fisheries who is a very resourceful man and I am sure therefore he is going to have a very good answer to this:
Today I was reminded that our sales to South America are off, and it was suggested that my trip may be the reason. May I say that the reason I went to South America was that our markets at that time were abnormally high. Since then dollar difficulties in several of the South American countries, particularly Brazil, have caused restrictions of exports from dollar countries.
I am going to be commendably brief, too. I shall be glad if the minister will make a note of that and perhaps comment on it later. He will no doubt deal more particularly with the question of prices, and include that among the other things which he comments on in his reply.

Mr. Chairman, hon. members who have spoken tonight have tried to be brief, and although it seems a little doubtful that we might finish with fisheries estimates today I shall try to be brief myself. I would wish, however, to congratulate the Minister of Fisheries on the presentation he made here today. I am not going to be a bit backward in doing that because I feel 83276-288
Supply-Fisheries
it was the finest presentation of fisheries that I have heard in the House of Commons in the nine years I have been here. At the same time I also wanted to say I believe that in the short time that he has been at the head of this department he has gained the confidence of those in the industry, including the tens of thousands of fishermen right across this country. They believe he is doing a good job, and I believe he is doing a good job.
In his remarks today the minister hit on one thing with which I would like to deal for a few minutes. The minister referred to the quality of fish being produced today and compared it with the quality of fish produced a few years ago. That, to my mind, is the key to the whole situation. In years gone by we did not have the equipment and were not in a position to send high quality fish into the cities in this country and in the United States, but with the help of the research board and other branches of the Department of Fisheries there has been a great improvement over the last few years. I believe that the inspection service which has been set up is doing a very good job in this regard. The thing for us to do now is to fight for better quality and when we do get that better quality there will be better markets, and I am sure we will have much happier fishermen.
I would like to address myself briefly to the situation within the industry generally and just emphasize a few points which the minister, in the short time at his disposal, did not have time to deal with. One hon. member a few moments ago pointed out that last year the fishermen were not looking forward to a very bright future. But I believe we have passed over that period and at the present time it would appear in the maritime provinces that the stocks of fish are practically cleaned off the shelves and out of the warehouses.
In the sardine industry, in which I am particularly interested, the only thing we have to worry about now is catching the sardines. The stocks that were on hand two years ago are completely exhausted but the price today is very reasonable and the demand is good. If we can now catch the sardines for the canneries I am sure our sardine fishermen will be happy once again.
On two occasions since I came to this house last November I have brought up the matter of loans for fishermen. I realize that this is an immense problem for the minister of the department in endeavouring to work out a plan which would provide loans for fishermen in all parts of Canada. However, I know that the minister has taken this matter under

Supply-Fisheries
consideration and I hope he may be able to devise some plan whereby these particular primary producers, when they find the going a little tough, will be able to borrow sufficient to enable them to carry on in that business that they, their lathers and forefathers have been in for so many years. We have had short periods of prosperity in the fishing industry, but to a greater extent we have had those periods when it is nothing but long hours, hard work, and insufficient returns for the amount of work and worry involved.
There is one other subject I wish to bring to the attention of the minister and I hope he will be able to give it his serious consideration. I believe that on the Atlantic coast line, in the bay of Fundy area particularly, we should have a scientific study to see if we can determine the cause of the great variation and irregularity in the catch of sardines such as we have had over the past few years. It may be a problem which is nearly insurmountable, but it is one which I believe can be solved. I am not going into this matter in detail, but I was in the sardine industry as a very young boy and I remember 1917 was a year of scarcity all over the bay of Fundy. We had an average year in 1918 and it carried on like that until 1923 when we again had a year of scarcity when we caught practically no sardines at all. We have had periods of plenty and even longer periods when we were unable to get sufficient sardines to take care of our costs.
Oil engines were first introduced when I was a boy and I remember that the fishermen in those days were convinced that the oil engines were responsible for the great decrease in the catch of sardines. Then as time went on other electrical devices were introduced into the sardine industry such as sounding equipment and some fishermen were convinced that they were responsible for the great decrease in the catch. Others are firmly convinced that winter seining is responsible for the great decrease in the catch in other years. But during the last sixteen months the catch of sardines in that area has been well below average and at the present time it is a great worry to the fishermen and to the canneries also who employ hundreds of men and women on that coast line.
If we could get some assistance from the fisheries department and from the research board in this type of survey I know it would be much appreciated by those in the canning industry and by the fishermen themselves. I am not criticizing the fact that we are furnishing funds in other parts of the world to make studies of a similar nature. I think they

are wonderful investments and I support them one hundred per cent. But I believe this is one particular branch of the industry which should have a thorough investigation and I believe it would be well worth while.
I would just like to refer briefly to a statement made in this house a few days ago by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. His name has been mentioned here today already. But in the speech he made when he set out to save many millions of dollars for the Canadian people he mentioned and criticized the fact that this government had-but perhaps I should read his remarks. He said as reported at page 4333 of Hansard:
In the year 1952-53, according to the public accounts, 20,000 Canadians were treated under the provisions of the act-
That would be the sick mariners act, as it is known on the coast line.
-and 89,000 foreign seamen. That year the cost of the service to the taxpayer was $588,000. Yet, the revenue collected on duties was only $340,000, or a net loss of about $250,000. Perhaps there are reasons why my suggestion would not be feasible, but it seems to me that it would be logical to increase the duties which are charged for this service until they cover the cost. If that could be done I suggest that the taxpayer could be saved in the neighbourhood of $250,000 a year.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw goes on to say that this would constitute a great saving which could be made for the Canadian people. I want to be fair at the outset and state most sincerely that I do not believe that the hon. member's statement meets with the approval of the majority of the members of the C.C.F. party.
You are quite correct in that statement.

But nevertheless the statement was made, though I do not believe the hon. member stopped to consider that this is a reciprocal agreement. If we had Canadian seamen in some foreign port without a dollar in their pockets and in need of hospital care or a doctor's attention then it would be provided under this agreement. I paid into this sick benefit fund for many years and I was fortunate enough never to be obliged to seek benefit under it and for that I am thankful. However, I do believe this is one matter the hon. member for Moose Jaw might well have left alone, particularly in view of the fact that he has strongly supported the building of the South Saskatchewan dam at a cost of well over $100 million. He has supported that project in the House of Commons even though competent engineers have decided that they could not make a favourable report on that project.

The hon. member has also suggested on various occasions since I have been in this house that a federal fund should be provided to supply fresh water for the city in which he lives. He has spoken on that matter on several occasions and all I can say is that in eastern Canada when we want a water supply in the cities and villages the taxpayers in the particular locality set out to provide it for themselves.
But in this case when the men who go down to the sea in ships are protected by this insurance fund the hon. member for Moose Jaw saw fit to criticize the fact that it was costing the taxpayers of this country $225,000 per year. Let me say at this point that I stood on my feet and supported a grant of $65 million for the western farmers of Canada and I would add that it would take something like 260 years, if my figures are correct, for that same amount to be claimed by the fishermen and seamen in this great country of ours.
Another comparison I might make while I have this matter in mind is that this sum mentioned by the hon. member would be only 50 per cent of the amount paid out in annual grants to the maple sugar producers of this country for the purchase of aluminum pails. I regret that the hon. member for Moose Jaw saw fit to suggest this great saving of $250,000 at the cost of those men who go out with no other protection than their own two hands, and that he would apparently deny them the protection which they have enjoyed for a great many years under this act.
I could point to individual cases with which I have had to deal over the past year in which men were hospitalized when they did not have a dollar to their name, and without this protection I am doubtful as to whether their families would have been able to carry on. I am sorry that the matter was ever raised in the House of Commons. If the hon. member for Moose Jaw had just taken a few minutes to get some particulars, not only in this case but in other cases that he mentioned, I am sure that he would not have put on record some of these great savings that he was going to make for the Canadian taxpayers.
I agree with you.

I was greatly
interested in one statement made by the Minister of Fisheries today. That was when he stated that 80 per cent of the fish and fish products of this country of ours must be exported. When my friend to my left, the hon. member for Greenwood, was speaking just a few minutes ago, I thought I might bring that matter to his mind. He and others 83276-2884

in the House of Commons-and I am not criticizing them for it because it is their belief-made a great plea for protection. There is a good example that I can bring to his attention tonight showing why I am bitterly opposed to protection. That example is that 20 per cent of what we produce in the fishing industry in this country is consumed in Canada.
Would the hon member permit a question?
Gladly.

I just want to ask him
if he is aware of the fact that the party to which I belong supported GATT and the trade which it sought to bring, throughout the years ever since it was brought in?

I am not disputing the hon. member's word, Mr. Chairman. But I have seen him get to his feet in the House of Commons since last November on two or three occasions and plead for these poor manufacturers of electrical appliances in Canada who are being so terribly pushed around.

Will the hon. member
permit another question? Did he ever hear me ask for an increase in tariffs?
I certainly did.
May I ask the hon. member when?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think I should point out to the committee that two hon. members cannot have the floor at once. The hon. member for Charlotte has the floor.

I am asking the hon.
gentleman if he will be good enough to look in Hansard. I am quite satisfied that he wil1 find no reference to an increase in tariffs made by me.

I cannot tell the hon. member the page of Hansard but when the legislation in connection with dumping in Canada was being discussed in this house the hon. gentleman to my left, standing where he stood just a minute ago, stated to the Minister of National Revenue that he was most hopeful that when this matter was under consideration those who manufacture electrical appliances in this country would not be forgotten. Is that asking for protection or is it not? I can find that in Hansard, and I shall be glad to do so tomorrow.
What I wanted to say was this. The figures put on record today by the Minister of Fisheries give a clear indication why the people down in the maritime provinces are bitterly opposed to protection. The matter was raised today by the Leader of the

Supply-Fisheries
Opposition when he was anxious to know from the Minister of Fisheries whether this statement in the press or over the radio was true with regard to embargoes that were being put on Canadian fish going into the United States. We have always enjoyed those markets in the United States. We have always had free entry into those markets in the United States. I can assure you that we appreciate them. I do not wish to see anything done in this country-and I realize that at the present time there are many people who want it-to create a feeling between those two countries which might bring about a tariff war. That is the last thing I want to see. The freer exchange of goods there is over this great boundary of 3,500 miles, the better we like it down there, This is just another example. There are many other commodities I could mention but they would not come under the matter we are now discussing. I could mention wood pulp and many other products which would be in the same category.
We are most dependent on foreign markets. For that reason we do not want to see anything done that would be harmful in any way to those markets which we have enjoyed for many years. I really hope to see the day when the barriers might be taken down completely. When that is done I believe you will see much more happiness on this side of the border. You will then see a much better chance of having a peaceful world to live in. As I have stated on many other occasions, the troubles we have encountered down through the years in too many cases have been brought about by one country refusing to do business with another. You can never have a happy and contented people when one is trying to be just a jump ahead of the other all the time in connection with tariffs.
There is just one other subject I will mention. I have now spoken much longer than I had intended to speak. In his remarks today the minister also mentioned the fact that out in British Columbia they had been most successful with the provincial legislature, the federal legislature and business generally in making arrangements which were agreeable to all concerned where rivers were being obstructed by dams for power purposes and others. This has been a problem down in our section of the country also, but to a much lesser extent than in British Columbia because our rivers are much smaller. However, I want to bring to the attention of the minister the St. Croix river which is the boundary line between the state of Maine and the province of New Brunswick, and in fact of Charlotte county. For many

years we enjoyed an extensive salmon industry on that river. Dams were built for mills that are operating there today. There was pollution which was never properly taken care of. For many years the river was neglected and it was considered perhaps to be a hopeless case. But the officials in the state of Maine have been interested in the project for quite some time and in a recent survey it was determined that the water there was "B" water, as I think it is called; at least it is water in which fish thrive without any worry.
I talked to some of these officials myself, and I have found that they are firmly convinced that this river can be made a great salmon river once again. Below the Canadian Cottons mill there is a fishway that has not been kept in repair for many years. In their estimation it would not be a costly matter to have that river put once more in a position so that salmon could go up the river. In their estimation it would mean hundreds of thousands of dollars to the citizens in that county if the river could again be opened for sport fishing. I would ask the minister to look into this matter carefully. I am sure he will find that the officials in the state of Maine are prepared to go ahead with this project at any time the department here would be interested in doing so.
I shall now resume my seat. But before doing so I again thank the minister for a most comprehensive statement. I am sure that the fishermen in the section from which I come will be most pleased to receive the story he had to tell in the House of Commons. I believe there are one or two more hon. members who wish to speak tonight; it is quite apparent that we shall not finish. However, I shall resume my seat at this time.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Mr. Chairman-

Before the minister replies, I should like to ask him two questions. The first one has to do with a submission that I received-and no doubt he received it also -from the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union about three months ago concerning the Japanese sending out expeditions to catch salmon in the vicinity of the Aleutian islands. It is apparently what is called an offshore salmon expedition. This submission shows that they are catching increasing numbers of salmon each year and indicates the fear that these particular salmon may be salmon which have spawned in British Columbia rivers and lakes. I should be glad if the minister would explain just

what the view of the department is on that particular question. The minister said this afternoon that the fishing is being done farther and farther out to sea. It may be just possible that this particular type of offshore fishing will affect our own coastal fishing very seriously.
The other question on which I would ask him to advise the committee has to do with the crab fishing in Hecate strait. As he knows, I raised that question last year. My information is that the Americans are taking a larger and larger proportion of the crabs from that strait. In fact one informant says that they will get 80 per cent of the crabs that are taken outside the three mile limit. Apparently Canadian fishermen cannot get their catch into the United States market without paying duty whereas American fishermen take these crabs from what we consider are Canadian waters and get them into the American market as American crabs. There is a fear that the whole crab fishery in Hecate strait will be ruined by the Americans. Apparently they are running short of crabs in their own waters and there is some danger that they will move into Hecate strait in a big way and clean out the fishery there.
I know there is a commission going into the whole question of what should be considered Canadian territorial waters, but I suggest to the minister that Hecate strait is really between two parts of Canada, the Queen Charlotte islands and the mainland, and should not be considered in the same light as territorial waters on the ocean itself. It does seem to me that Canada should take the position that Hecate strait is Canadian territorial waters. Other nations have taken a similar position in recent years. I have a list here of quite a few countries. Referring to one of the bulletins of the fisheries council of Canada, I see that the Australian government, for example, apparently has imposed strict territorial control over pearl fishing in the waters on the continental shelf. Other countries have taken a stand.
The present government policy seems to be to wait for the report of the commission and then after that take up the question at the United Nations. By the time we get all that rigmarole finished there will be no crab fishing left in Hecate strait. I do suggest with regard to that particular strait that it should be possible for Canada to take the position that these are Canadian territorial waters.
Would the minister be kind enough to permit a brief question before he answers? Will he make a statement clarifying the significance of the news report from Washington this afternoon-

I have already been asked.
Supply-Fisheries
Yes, by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, but I should like clarification particularly as to what effect, if any, this will have on the export of lobsters to the United States.

In view of the Japan-United States-Canada treaty, perhaps the minister would like to explain to the house if anything is being done of an exploratory nature in the search for other areas of fishing on the Pacific coast.

In the fifteen minutes left I will try to touch quickly on the main points raised by various members. First of all I want to express my appreciation for the many kind things said. It was refreshing to have my friend from Cape Breton and my friend, the financial critic, the hon. member for Greenwood, bring me down to earth with the remarks they made. I completely agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South that whatever has been done in the fisheries department has been due mainly to the very excellent staff in our department, in the research stations and on our international commissions.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich spoke first and asked what we were doing about the inspection of fish on boats and packers. It is quite true that that is the place where some careless handling does occur. At the moment what we are trying to do is to step up our inspection of plants. The co-operation of the provinces is necessary in that because they do the licensing of these plants, but we expect in the next year to have very much closer inspection in the plants themselves, and that of course will apply to the fish going through the plants. Perhaps at a later stage we may actually get to the inspection of the fish on the boats.
As far as territorial waters are concerned, several members have raised the question. It is quite true that we have a special legal committee making our submission to the government on the matter, but in the meantime two of the extensions in other countries to which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra referred are being taken to the international court. It is easy for a country to shove out its boundaries and declare that their boundaries are farther out, but other countries, who have had historic rights to fish these waters protest that action. I do not think that any action will be taken until there is a decision, if the case of Britain and Iceland is taken to the international court, the case which has given rise to this whole question. A country like ours, which has valuable inshore fisheries, is naturally anxious to have more than a three mile limit.

Supply-Fisheries
That is one of the reasons we keep our own trawlers twelve miles out, to show other people that we do believe we should have control out to twelve miles.
The hon. member for New Westminster asked me whether, when the closure goes into effect on a portion of the Fraser river, the fishermen who are prevented from fishing there will be allowed to fish elsewhere. They will be so allowed. At the present time they are of course restricted to their own part of the river during the open season.
The hon. member for Gloucester asked whether or not we could not give a warning of changes in the regulations. We do that on the west coast. Every year the whole industry, fishermen, fish plants, our scientists and the sport fishermen, send their suggestions for changes in the regulations to the department. We print all those and circulate them without comment. Then the comment comes in, and at the end of that period we make our decisions on changes. We are going to start a similar process on the east coast.
The hon. member also mentioned the oyster development on the east coast. Oysters are one of the few fish which we cannot produce in sufficient abundance for our own market. We certainly are anxious to increase our oyster production in Canada in every way We can.
The senior member for Halifax and the hon. members for Trinity-Conception and Gloucester all mentioned the matter of our trawlers. We do keep our big trawlers twelve miles offshore. We do this partly because we believe that is where our territorial waters should be and also to give our smaller drag-gers a better chance inshore. Of the three members who spoke one wanted the trawlers kept out and the other two wanted the trawlers let in. However, that policy is under study today.
Several members spoke about unemployment insurance. The Minister of Labour is conducting a further study and the fisheries department of course is offering all the facilities of our department to aid in that study.
May I ask a question with respect to the twelve mile limit? I was not quite clear whether the minister said we were respecting that as a matter of principle or just for the larger vessels.

As far as we ourselves are concerned, we keep our large vessels, the Canadian trawlers, twelve miles out. The embarrassing thing is that other nations can bring their trawlers up to our three mile limit because they are on the high seas. We have no control over them on the high seas,
IMr. Sinclair.]
but having control over our own ships we keep the big trawlers out twelve miles.
The hon. member for Queens asked me about the increase, if any, in the lobster catch. The lobster is like the salmon on the west coast. It is a completely controlled fishery. We think we are just about at maximum production now because of the even level of the catch in recent years. What we are trying to do now is to increase the size of the lobsters caught by a slight increase in the legal size.
The hon. member for Halifax spoke very glowingly of our experimental station in Halifax, which is one of the best in this part of the world, and on the work that has been done. He asked for an improvement in the guardian service on the rivers. We are increasing our seasonal protection staff in the Atlantic provinces in line with the increased conservation program that we are launching with the provinces.
The hon. member for Trinity-Conception seemed to suggest that I was spending more time on the west coast than I was in the maritimes. The whole fisheries department, I think, spends much more time on the problems of the east coast, especially those of Newfoundland. The west coast is a highly organized fishery. Both the operators and the fishermen are highly organized and they pretty well take care of themselves. It is in Newfoundland and on the Atlantic coast that most of the fishery problems seem to arise.
He mentioned the depressed state of the salt cod industry. It is quite true that we are taking a first class fish, processing it in a rather primitive way that has not changed much in 400 years and then selling it in low price markets of the world, the Mediterranean and the Caribbean areas. We are trying to get away from that in our development program. We are trying to get more and more of that cod turned into fresh and frozen form and sold in the highest priced markets of the world, Canada and the United States. This fish stick development will certainly be of great aid in that.
Then, there was the matter of the capelins. The capelin does come in millions, and it is a very tasty little fish in the fresh state. It is very like the eulachon. It is, however, a very oily fish and it is difficult to preserve, but it does serve as the main food for cod.
My friend asked for the names of the members of the trade delegation over in Spain and Portugal now. There is Mr. Bull, the deputy minister of trade and commerce; Mr. Schwartzman, a tariff expert from trade and commerce; and Mr. Laws, the secretary-manager of NAFEL. They are there negotiating on tariffs. The actual signing committee

which will go later will be made up of the Minister of Public Works and my deputy, Mr. Bates.
The hon. member asked also for an increase in herring exploration on the west coast of Newfoundland. We have done quite a bit of work on herrings in the gulf of St. Lawrence. There is still a great deal to be learned about the herring runs there and the sardine runs. This is one of the reasons for switching of the heads of the biological research stations. Dr. Hart, on the west coast station at Nanaimo, who has had a great deal of experience with herring and salmon, is being transferred to the east coast station at St. Andrews. Dr. Needier from there is being moved to the west coast because he has had a great deal of experience on international commissions. We want to make studies in British Columbia on ground-fish and crustaceans.
Then the hon. member for Comox-Alberni spoke about the problem of dams. It is quite true that it is not an easy problem to get the spawning fish up past the dam, but it is a much more difficult problem to get the little fingerlings down. Often in going over the dam they are dashed to death, and if they go through the spillways about 25 per cent are lost because of skin burns. Our research people and those in the United States and on the commissions have done a great deal of work on guiding fingerlings down the ladders by sound, by light and by electronic impulses. Progress is being made, although we have no certain solution as yet.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond asked me to help him with some public works project relating to fishermen. The final decision, of course, rests in the hands of my colleague, the Minister of Public Works. I hope to press forward with those developments that are of help to the whole industry, and not just individual ridings. He mentioned the hope that we would use a helicopter to curb poaching in the one area in which it is apt to be most prevalent, the Queen Charlotte islands. We have that under consideration. We are using two helicopters in Newfoundland because of the transportation trouble we have down there. If in Newfoundland we build too large a patrol boat it cannot get into the harbours, and if we build a small one it will not stand the Atlantic storms. The hon. member spoke of a good man, Rothery, we have as fishery officer. In fact, he is so good we are moving
Supply-Fisheries
him to the supervisor's office in Vancouver, so the hon. member may be losing him.
The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador spoke about the decline in schooner fishing on the banks on both the east and west coasts; we should like to get more of our fishermen out deep-sea fishing. For too long a time now most of our men have been shore fishermen. We have two of the greatest fisheries in the world on our coasts and if we do not fully exploit them other nations will come and fish those waters. We hope to have more offshore Canadian boats out instead of so many shore fishermen.
The member for Cape Breton South spoke about a change in fishing practices and the mechanization of the industry. He asked about the effect of the United States tariff commission announcement made public today. This problem with United States tariffs-it is just on ground fish like cod and haddock fillets-was aggravated by a territorial waters dispute between Britain and Iceland. As a result of that dispute the British fish trade refused to handle Icelandic fish, so the fish came in unusually great quantities to the United States. Our own relations with the United States have been very good. We both serve the same North American markets, have the same wage scales, and so on. I do not think the full details of that United States tariff commission announcement have been reported as yet.
I have heard that the Icelandic fish is now going to Russia. Is that correct?

I understand some of it is, and some of it is now going back into Britain.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare spoke about the need for an insurance plan to cover boats and lobster traps. Perhaps I could answer that question when we come to the item in the estimates covering losses. He asked about the success of steel traps for lobsters. Big steel traps are used very successfully for crabs on the west coast, but on the east coast the old wooden traps which they make are still used. We are experimenting with the steel traps, but the experiments have not gone far enough to make any statement on the matter.
The hon. member for Greenwood was asking whether prices were really so good that everyone was making a lot of money in the fishing business. They are not. Everything in this world is comparative. They are just

Supply-Fisheries
better than they were last year. The fishermen, like the farmers, are optimists and as long as there is an uptrend everything is fine.
Mention was made of the fact that we used to have a good market for salt cod in Brazil. For some years the market was closed. But recently the Brazil government did again make dollars available for buying salted cod. I am sorry, but I cannot explain the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on South American trade. Perhaps he can explain the remarks he made.
The member for Charlotte spoke of the need for high quality of fish and also the need for loans to fishermen, and I shall say a word on that a little later. He dealt with the irregular catch of sardines, and that is related to the herring problem in the gulf and off the west coast of Newfoundland. I hope we will do more research on these. We have got our research pretty well in shape in British Columbia so that we can forecast fairly accurately the herring run, and we should be able to do that on the Atlantic coast.
The member for Vancouver-Quadra asked two questions about the fishermen's union's statement that the Japanese were again fishing off our shores. The main point of the new north Pacific treaty is that for the next ten years, five years certain and five years in review, the Japanese agree to stay on their side of the ocean, in so far as these species of fish which are thoroughly studied, fully exploited and thoroughly protected are concerned-the salmon, herring and halibut. Despite the traditional freedom of the sea the Japanese agreed to abstain from fishing those three species on our side of the ocean. As an indication may I say that in the peak year before the war the Japanese caught 200 million salmon in the whole Pacific, and last year they caught 7 million on their own side under the treaty.
It came down from 200 million to 7 million?

Yes, that is when they fished the whole ocean, and they caught 7 million last year on their own side.
We are anxious to see this treaty a success. The only way we will know what salmon go to Siberia and Japan and the Canadian and American rivers is by a study. This study is to be made by the north Pacific 
commission of which Mr. Bates is chairman. The commission met in Washington, and their first scientific studies are starting in Tokyo this month. We hope to find the answer to where this dividing line is in the Pacific between the two stocks of salmon.
Then, there was the question of territorial waters, and I have covered it. We have always said that Hecate strait is Canadian territorial waters by the declaration of 1908 or 1909. Despite incidents, we have never taken the United States fishermen to court about it, even though they fish those waters. Probably if nationals of other countries did so, we would take them to court.
Has the minister any figures on the crab fishery?

I will have them when I come back.
The last question asked by the member for Victoria, B.C., was what we were doing about fishing on the high seas. Well, we are trying to encourage our fishermen to go out to sea, but most of our fishing boats on the west coast have been suited only for inland waters. They do most of their fishing in sheltered waters because the salmon and other fish come in to the coast and rivers.
The B.C. industry said it was too great a risk to build expensive boats for deep-sea fishing which may or may not be successful. They said they could get some boats at a reasonable price from the tuna and sardine fisheries in the United States. These boats are available at a reasonable price. We have permitted our industry to bring in 15 of these boats for a trial effort, to get out to sea and catch more salmon, to find tuna and to do the sort of fishing that fishing nations should do.
If this experiment is a success, then there will probably be new boats built in Canadian yards. In the meantime our Canadian yards will get work, and it will be a lot of work, in refitting these boats for deep-sea fishing.
That is on the east coast?

No. on the west coast. We want to get our boats out to deep-sea fishing off British Columbia. That covers most of the questions raised. There are one or two specific questions I will answer when we come to the particular items affected.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
